entries.proposition: The primary endpoint pooled convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome and drop seizures in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome into one combined population, measured in the maintenance period.
entries.snippet: The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in frequency of convulsive seizures (DS) or drop seizures (LGS) in patients receiving soticlestat in the combined patient population during the maintenance period, compared with those receiving placebo.

entries.proposition: The two populations were combined to increase power, with about 23 Dravet and 40 Lennox-Gastaut patients planned per arm.
entries.snippet: The two patient populations were combined for the primary endpoint analysis to increase the power of the study.

entries.proposition: The statistical analysis plan specified an efficacy analysis set for the primary analysis; the report uses the more inclusive modified intent-to-treat set instead.
entries.snippet: An efficacy analysis set, comprising a subset of the mITT analysis set, was specified in the study statistical analysis plan for the primary endpoint analysis.

entries.proposition: Primary result: placebo-adjusted median reduction of 30.21 percent in the combined population (p 0.0008).
entries.snippet: soticlestat demonstrated a placebo‐adjusted median reduction in seizure frequency of 30.21% (95% CI = −45.97% to −13.88%) during the maintenance period (p = .0008; Figure 3A).

entries.proposition: Dravet subgroup: placebo-adjusted median reduction 50.00 percent (p 0.0002); Lennox-Gastaut: 17.08 percent, not significant.
entries.snippet: Patients with DS who received soticlestat demonstrated a statistically significant placebo‐adjusted median reduction in convulsive seizure frequency of 50.00% (95% CI = −74.15% to −24.68%, p = .0002) over the maintenance period

entries.proposition: Responders with at least 50 percent reduction in Dravet syndrome: 30.8 percent on drug against 0 percent on placebo.
entries.snippet: This reduction was observed in 30.8% of patients with DS who received soticlestat versus 0% of those who received placebo

entries.proposition: Baseline drop-seizure frequency in the Lennox-Gastaut arms differed several-fold (mean 440.98 against 150.02) with very wide ranges.
entries.snippet: However, the baseline frequency for drop seizures in patients with LGS was more varied, with mean frequencies in the soticlestat and placebo groups of 440.98 (SD = 1133.542) and 150.02 (SD = 203.822), respectively (Table 1).

entries.proposition: The authors say differences in baseline drop-seizure frequency suggest the drop-seizure definition was implemented differently.
entries.snippet: the observed differences in baseline seizure frequency, in otherwise similar populations as defined by inclusion/exclusion criteria, suggest a difference in how the definition of drop seizure was implemented.

entries.proposition: Global functioning was assessed by investigator and caregiver impression-of-change scales.
entries.snippet: Global functioning was evaluated using the investigator‐ and caregiver‐reported Clinical Global Impression of Change (CGI‐C and Care GI‐C, respectively)

entries.proposition: The Discussion states that global functioning was shown to improve with drug although the figure p-values are 0.06 to 0.11 apart from one 0.039.
entries.snippet: Global functioning was shown to improve with soticlestat treatment, with investigators and caregivers reporting a greater improvement with soticlestat than with placebo.

entries.proposition: Plasma 24HC fell within two weeks and stayed lower; the authors say this indicates target engagement.
entries.snippet: These findings indicate engagement of soticlestat with CH24H, which is predominantly expressed in the brain, resulting in the observed systemic reductions of 24HC.

entries.proposition: The authors note that 24HC fell similarly in both syndromes while a significant seizure reduction occurred only in Dravet syndrome.
entries.snippet: Although soticlestat treatment reduced plasma 24HC levels in both the DS and the LGS patient groups, a significant reduction in seizure frequency was only observed in patients with DS.

entries.proposition: The authors state that, although early effective intervention may improve long-term developmental outcomes by reducing epileptic activity, treatment goals should go beyond seizures.
entries.snippet: Although early and effective intervention may potentially improve long‐term developmental outcomes by reducing epileptic activity, treatment goals should also go beyond seizure control and aim to address the nonseizure symptoms as well

entries.proposition: The authors state the results may not be generalisable to a real-world population.
entries.snippet: However, given the clinical trial setting, the results reported here may not be generalizable to a real‐world population.

entries.proposition: Supplement: myoclonic and atypical-absence seizure-free days were similar between arms (73.26 and 72.07 percent), the safety check that the drug did not worsen those seizure types.
